items.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003
items.q: And it also had Count Basie’s “One O’clock Jump” on it which I liked a lot.

ctx.x: It was a way of connecting. I was not also taken with pop vocal music. It just didn’t — I liked the rhythm & blues sound, I don’t know why, the hoarseness maybe of some of the masculine baritone singers. I remember “Duke of Earl” very well, or “Alley-Oop” the Coasters. These are the kinds of songs that I liked. I was not into the ballads. I didn’t care about Johnny Mathis that was hot at the time. I don’t think I had been exposed to Jackie Wilson then. One of the first jazz vocals that I really remember, and this…

parents’ records, was Doris Day singing “Sentimental Journey” with Les Brown. And I really liked that. And it was on a sampler. Lucky Strike put out some sort of “This is Jazz” LP. And it also had Count Basie’s “One O’clock Jump” on it which I liked a lot. And that sort of mystified me because it didn’t have a melody at the beginning.
